audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: Identity: Westerlund's Ngarla is the Ngayarta (Pilbara, Port Hedland) language = Glottolog ngar1296; no languoid confusion. Quote: confirmed verbatim at the stated place (sec. 2.3, Table 7, p.10) in the ANU open-access PDF, fetched sources now because the record held no file. Coding: rule '10 100 1010 10010 101010' reproduces Table 7 exactly (initial main stress; secondary on the penult in 4-5 syllable words, 3rd+5th in 6-syllable words), so 'fixed-dominant, initial' stands. strict=false/dom=true is also right: the source itself lists lexical exceptions (three long suffixes carry their own main stress on their 2nd syllable) and the Geytenbeek pronunciation guide relayed in Westerlund 2007 p.72 adds a predictable phonetic exception (initial-vowel elision in /k p t/+/i u/+/r w/ sequences shifts stress to the next vowel, pirirri -> 'pri:rri'). Source quality: the deciding work is the only reference

sources.citation: Westerlund 2015, A Grammatical Sketch of Ngarla, sec. 2.3 (ANU repository PDF, full text extracted 2026-08-31)
sources.quote: Stress in Ngarla is predictable. [Table 7:] One to three syllable words: Main stress on 1st syllable, no secondary stress. Four syllable words: ... secondary stress on 3rd syllable. Five syllable words: ... secondary stress on 4th syllable. Six syllable words: ... secondary stress on 3rd and 5th syllables.

sources.citation: Westerlund, Torbjörn. 2015. A grammatical sketch of Ngarla (Ngayarta, Pama-Nyungan). Asia-Pacific Linguistics A-PL 16. Canberra: Australian National University. hdl.handle.net/1885/14712
sources.quote: 'Stress in Ngarla is predictable. ... According to Geytenbeek (2006), the stress placement rules of Ngarla are as shown in Table 7' [1-3 syll: main stress on 1st, no secondary; 4 syll: secondary on 3rd; 5 syll: secondary on 4th; 6 syll: secondary on 3rd and 5th]; suffixes -kujarra, -rukarra, -pungkara 'have their own main stress, which invariably falls on the second syllable'; p.39 'main stress always falls on the first syllable of a word'.
sources.locator: sec. 2.3 p.10 (PDF p.22), Table 7; also sec. 4 p.39

sources.citation: Westerlund, Torbjörn. 2007. A grammatical sketch of Ngarla: A language of Western Australia. MA thesis, Uppsala University (also issued by Wangka Maya PALC), 72 pp. (Wayback copy of www2.lingfil.uu.se/ling/semfiler/)
sources.quote: 'As a primary rule stress should be placed on the first syllable of each word ... In words of four or five syllables, the second-to-last syllable is also stressed, though more lightly than the first. A predictable exception occurs only in words of five or more phonemes, and only when sequences within such words begin with /k/, /p/, or /t/, are followed by /i/ or /u/, and then by /r/ or /w/. In such cases the first vowel is shortened or even omitted, and if there would have been stress on that vowel it is transferred onto the next vowel' (e.g. pirirri -> "pri:rri", kuwarri -> "kwa:rri").
sources.locator: Appendix 'Pronunciation guidelines for the phonemic alphabet used for the Aboriginal languages of eastern Pilbara', p.72, 'adapted from Geytenbeek 2006a:6'
